# The machine and long runs

## The machine

- 4 CPUs (Intel Xeon; the clock differs between sessions, 2.1 or 2.8 GHz), about 15 GB of memory, no swap. JDK 25 at `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` (21 is installed too).
- The suites use the four cores by running four JVMs of 768 MB each at one interpreter thread; the distance stage holds one core and 4 GB for 13 to 24 minutes. Run nothing else when a number is to be kept.
- Disk: every run that imports a grammar leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! parser directory, `fortress<random>rats`, in the JVM's temporary directory (`/tmp` by default), and never deletes it; hundreds of them once filled the allowance and broke tool output with "no space left on device". Check `df -h /` before a long run. Sourcing `env.sh` deletes `/tmp/fortress*rats`, so source it once per shell and never while another agent's run may be using them; point your own runs' `java.io.tmpdir` at your tree's `tmp/` (`build-and-caches.md`).
- Absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions: the same tree has measured 40 % slower in another session.

## Long commands

The Bash tool kills a foreground call at 10 minutes (2 by default). `ant testFast`, the distance stage and the gate are longer. Start a long command in the background with a log, and poll the log. Never pipe `ant`, or any long command, through `tail`: the verdict is at the end, and you would have to run it again to see it. Grep the log instead.

    run_bg () {      # run_bg <logfile> "<command>"
        nohup bash -c "( $2 ) > '$1' 2>&1; echo EXIT=\$? >> '$1'" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    }
    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
        done
        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    }

Keep each wait inside the prompt cache's life: five minutes for a subagent, an hour for the main session. A wait past it makes the next call write the agent's whole context again (`agents-and-recovery.md`). So a subagent polls in steps under about four and a half minutes and never chains sleeps in one call past that, or hands the run to a script and ends its turn. The `Monitor` tool can also watch a long run.

Stop or kill only processes under your own tree's path (`readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the path in their arguments), never by a script's name across the machine: other agents run copies of the same scripts.
----------
# Agents, stops, restarts and recovery

## Agents

- The Workflow harness runs two agents at a time; more wait for a free slot. Two building agents share the four cores.
- An agent costs about 45K tokens before it does anything. Agents started in parallel share the cache for the system prompt and tools only; an identical whole prompt is shared whole; a prompt that differs in its last line shares only the system prompt and tools. Text every agent of a kind needs can go in a project agent type's system prompt (`.claude/agents/<name>.md`), which agents of that type then read from the cache; a type written during a session is found only after the session's process restarts.
- The prompt cache lives one hour for the main session and five minutes for a subagent. A call within the life reads the cache and renews it; a wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again. Cost is counted as tokens written (cache writes and new input); cache reads are not counted.
- An agent call can return null even after the agent delivered its structured output: the API's safety filter can end an agent on a false positive, and the harness then marks it failed. Treat null like a thrown error: look at what the attempt left (its branch, its tree) and retry with that.
- `node --check` does not check a Workflow script the way the harness parses it, as the body of an async function. To check one: replace `export const meta` with `const meta` and pass the text to `new (Object.getPrototypeOf(async function(){}).constructor)(text)`.
- The automatic permission check refuses some steps, for example landing work on an earlier gate than the record names, or turning off the platform's git-check Stop hook, even after Pavol's go in chat. A refused outcome is not pursued by another tool or in a later turn. Switching to manual approval is Pavol's to do, and in manual mode an agent's commands wait for his approval.
- A worker whose context is compacted re-reads its brief from the first message of its own transcript. The boot sequence the compaction hook asks for is the coordinator's.

## Stops, restarts and recovery

What stops running work:

- The platform stops the session's process after about 12 h 58 min of continuous running, and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. The next stop is the last start plus 12 h 58 min: `uptime -s` gives the start, and `/tmp/env-manager.log` shows each stop as a SIGTERM.
- A VM restart: `uptime -s` changes; the disk survives.
- An interrupt of the coordinating session's turn (the stop button): every background agent alive at that moment dies. A message sent while the session is busy is queued and kills nothing, and a manual compaction between turns kills nothing.

After a restart, the conversation and session, the worktrees, uncommitted edits, untracked files, transcripts, each Workflow run's journal, and shell scripts started in the background are all still there. Every Workflow run and its agents, every Agent-tool worker and any push loop are gone. The platform's git-check Stop hook is back on: it makes the session take another turn whenever the tree has uncommitted, untracked or unpushed work.

Recovering:

1. Read what is on disk and what is pushed before doing anything: `git log`, `git status` in each worktree, the logs. A log that ended complete stands unless the tree changed after it; continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed. A command started in the background may still be running: find it by its log (no `EXIT=` line yet) or by a process under your tree's path, and wait for it instead of starting a second one.
2. A Workflow run is resumed, not relaunched: the same script and arguments, byte for byte, with `resumeFromRunId`. Agents that had finished keep their results; an unfinished one runs again from its start and finds its tree's leftovers. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls in call order: a base given as a short hash where the launch gave the full one misses from the first call. A script changed since the launch is resumed from a copy of the script as launched (`git show <commit>:<path>`). The run's journal is `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/journal.jsonl`: one `launched` line, a `started` line per agent call, a `result` line per agent that returned. `explorations/coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` reads it.
3. An Agent-tool worker stopped by a restart continues on a `SendMessage`. One killed by an interrupt cannot be resumed: it is relaunched only at Pavol's explicit ask, and the new worker is told its predecessor's leftovers.
4. A new session cannot resume another session's run. Its pushed work and the record carry over; nothing else does.
5. A session that must keep running is kept busy by check-ins: a series of one-shot `send_later` reminders armed together, 45 minutes apart (cron triggers allow an hour at the shortest, and about ten trigger creations a minute is the limit). One armed a few minutes after the predicted stop resumes what the stop killed.

Nothing that takes hours lives only on disk: commit and push as you go (`committing.md`). The transcript backup runs at the end of each turn of the main session, not when an agent finishes, so a session inside one long turn is not being backed up.

# Committing and pushing

Pavol decides what gets committed. Commit only when your task says to; a step his yes already covers is taken without asking again.

## What may be committed

- Committed: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script that is reusable.
- Never: captured outputs, logs, raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists, or any other scratch. Scratch lives under your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored; a private cache directory outside `tmp/` is not.
- Never: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable, Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck (`research/decks/` is gitignored; cite such a source by its Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief attributed quotations); `HANDOVER.md` or ZIP contents without Pavol's go. His email is for attribution only.
- No self-credit anywhere committed. Provenance and rationale go in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Never the deletion of `default_repository/caches/global.map` that every `ant compileAll` makes: restore it with `git checkout -- default_repository/caches/global.map`.

## How

- Commit only the paths you wrote, as you go, in one command, never a directory copy and never `git add -A`:

      git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- Read a staged change of more than a few hundred lines with `git diff --cached --stat` before committing it.
- An edit under the original tree (anything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`): the test is the first commit, alone (`tests-writing.md`), and the commit message flags the edit as one of the original tree.
- The footer, exactly as the protocol gives it. It names no model, whatever another footer the harness suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

## Pushing

- A worker on its own branch pushes that branch as it works (`git push -u origin <branch>` the first time), so that a lost container loses nothing. It never touches the main tree, `/home/user/fortress`.
- To `main`: only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing but your own commits, and then both, in this order:

      git push origin main
      git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8

  The second keeps current the branch the container is re-provisioned from; if it falls behind or disappears, a re-provisioned session starts stale or fails. No other branch is pushed without permission (the transcript branches excepted).

     1	<!-- How this work survives its container: the transcript backup mechanism, how to re-arm it in a fresh container, and how to recover a session whose container died. Written 2026-09-18 after the coordinating session of 2026-09-17 was lost mid-workflow; the incident and what it cost are recorded at the end. Specific to Claude Code running in a remote Anthropic container, not to Fortress. -->
     2	
     3	# The container, the transcripts, and recovery
     4	
     5	A session in this setup is a conversation in a remote container that can be
     6	reclaimed or corrupted at any time, and is re-provisioned by cloning a branch.
     7	Three things therefore have to be true at all times: the work is pushed, the
     8	transcript is pushed, and the branch the infrastructure clones is current.
     9	
    10	## What is where
    11	
    12	| thing | where | note |
    13	|---|---|---|
    14	| the work | `main`, and the container's infrastructure branch | both kept at the same commit, see *The branch trap* |
    15	| session transcripts | orphan branches `transcripts` and `transcripts-blinded` | no shared history with `main`; large blobs live only there |
    16	| live transcripts on disk | `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/` | `<session>.jsonl`, plus per-session directories |
    17	| the snapshot scripts | `<worktree>/scripts/` on each orphan branch — **these are the copies that run** | reference copy in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` |
    18	| the backup's log and state | `<worktree>/.backup.log`, `.backup.state`, `.backup.lock`, `.backup.pending` | never committed (the branch's `.gitignore`: `/.backup.*`) |
    19	
    20	Two orphan branches exist because the blinded microGPT runs were a controlled
    21	experiment: neither run's container was to hold the other's transcripts.
    22	`transcripts` holds the coordinating sessions, `transcripts-blinded` the
    23	blinded-run container's. Keep them apart; join them at analysis time, which
    24	costs nothing — see *Reading another session's transcript*.
    25	
    26	## How the snapshot works
    27	
    28	A `Stop` hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` runs `<worktree>/scripts/backup.sh`
    29	at the end of every assistant turn. Since `transcripts-blinded@974d9be7`
    30	(2026-09-29) the hook returns at once: it records a request
    31	(`.backup.pending`) and, unless a runner already holds the lock
    32	(`.backup.lock`, taken with `flock`), starts `backup.sh --run` detached in the
    33	background, and exits 0. The runner makes one pass per request until none is
    34	left. `backup_transcripts.py` copies the live JSONL into the worktree with two
    35	policy redactions (deck page images, HANDOVER.md contents); the runner then
    36	commits `projects/`, pushes whenever the branch is ahead of its upstream
    37	(retrying after 2, 4, 8 and 16 s), and packs loose objects. Each pass writes
    38	one line to `<worktree>/.backup.log`, the last 200 kept: its time, the
    39	copier's time and exit code, the commit, how far the branch was ahead, and the
    40	push's result. The copier is incremental: `.backup.state` records each
    41	source's size and modification time and the files written for it, and a
    42	source whose record and snapshot files still match is skipped without being
    43	read. A pass takes about 10 s (8.5 to 11.7 s between 17:50 and 18:00 UTC on
    44	2026-09-29, the copier about 1 s of it). These properties matter:
    45	
    46	- **It fires on the main session's Stop, not on any agent's completion.** A
    47	  session that sits inside one long turn is not being backed up, however much
    48	  work its agents are doing. This is the single largest gap in the design.
    49	- **It swallows every error and never holds up the session**, so a failing
    50	  push is silent. Read the `push=` field of the last line of `.backup.log`, or
    51	  `git -C <worktree> status -sb`.
    52	- **It snapshots every session in the container**, not just the current one.
    53	- **A container that dies within about 10 s of a turn ending loses that turn's
    54	  snapshot**: the pass runs after the hook has returned, and takes that long.
    55	- **Only `index.lock` is cleaned automatically.** A git process killed
    56	  mid-command leaves its lock behind. The runner removes an `index.lock` at
    57	  least 10 s old that no process has open, and waits out a younger one. A
    58	  stale lock on the branch's ref, `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock`
    59	  (the worktree shares the main repository's refs), is not cleaned: every
    60	  later commit fails on it, `commit=failed` in the log, until it is removed by
    61	  hand, after checking that no git process is running.
    62	- A `SessionStart` hook with matcher `compact` (2026-09-27, on Pavol's yes) injects, after every compaction, the instruction to boot by `coordinator/README.md` before anything else. It is in the tracked `.claude/settings.json` and in `~/.claude/settings.json`; a fresh container copies the second from the first.
    63	- The platform's own Stop hook, `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`, posts reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work after a turn. It comes from the launcher: the session's process is started with `--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`, whose `Stop` hook runs that script, and the script is rewritten at every process start. At Pavol's request on 2026-09-29 it was replaced by a no-op that reads its input and exits 0; the original is kept in the session scratchpad, `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`. It returns at each restart of the process, and turning it off again is Pavol's to do, in manual mode: the auto-mode permission check refused scheduling it. The coordinator's push loop covers what it protected: `autopush.sh` in the same scratchpad, every 4 minutes, pushes `main` and the container branch when every unpushed commit touches only `explorations/`, and otherwise pushes `main` to `wip/main-backup` only, so that a container reset loses nothing and `main` stays gated; it is started again after a process restart. While the hook is back, its reminders are advisory, declined without a word while held or gated changes exist, and never mentioned to Pavol.
    64	
    65	## Re-arming it in a fresh container
    66	
    67	```sh
    68	git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded transcripts-blinded
    69	# then register the Stop hook in ~/.claude/settings.json:
    70	#   {"hooks":{"Stop":[{"hooks":[{"type":"command",
    71	#     "command":"/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh"}]}]}}
    72	/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh --run   # one pass, in the foreground
    73	tail -1 /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log       # verify
    74	```
    75	
    76	The verify step: the log's last line reads `copier_rc=0` and either
    77	`commit=<hash>` with `push=ok`, or, when nothing changed since the last pass,
    78	`commit=none ahead=0 push=none`; `git -C <worktree> status -sb` shows the
    79	branch not ahead of its upstream. Run by hand, `--run` waits for any runner at
    80	work and then makes a pass. The hook's own form, without `--run`, returns at
    81	once, and its pass shows in the log about 10 s later.
    82	
    83	`explorations/experiment/setup.sh` does this for the blinded lineage. Substitute
    84	`transcripts` for the coordinating lineage, whose `scripts/` are still those of
    85	2026-09-17: copy the reference copies in first. The script that runs is the one in
    86	the worktree, on the branch — if you edit the reference copy under
    87	`explorations/`, nothing changes until it is copied into the worktree.
    88	
    89	## Three traps, each of which has cost us work
    90	
    91	**The workflow-transcript glob.** Agents launched by the `Workflow` tool do not
    92	write where `Agent`-tool subagents do. Their transcripts, the run journal and
    93	the persisted scripts live at
    94	
    95	```
    96	projects/<proj>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/agent-*.jsonl, journal.jsonl, *.meta.json
    97	projects/<proj>/<session>/workflows/scripts/<name>-<run>.js
    98	```
    99	
   100	one level below the `subagents/*.jsonl` glob that the script used until
   101	2026-09-18. Four workflow agents' transcripts — about 798k tokens — were
   102	therefore never captured. Fixed; the fixture test in the commit message of
   103	`transcripts-blinded@264d19c8` states what was verified.
   104	
   105	**The 100 MiB blob limit.** A snapshot rewrites the whole JSONL, so a long
   106	session's transcript grows past GitHub's per-blob ceiling and the push fails —
   107	silently, per above. A transcript over 64 MiB is now written as
   108	`<session>.jsonl.parts/NNN.jsonl`, cut at line boundaries so that appends leave
   109	every earlier part byte-identical. Rejoin with `cat <session>.jsonl.parts/*.jsonl`.
   110	
   111	**The loose-object pile.** The container's clone ships `gc.auto=0`, and each
   112	snapshot writes whole files with no delta, so the object store grows by tens of
   113	megabytes per commit: 21.3 GiB of loose objects by 2026-09-17, which packed down
   114	to 609 MB. `backup.sh` now ends with `git -c gc.auto=1000 gc --auto`, run with
   115	the runner's lock closed: until 2026-09-29 the detached `git gc` inherited the
   116	lock and held it for as long as it ran, and every snapshot requested meanwhile
   117	was silently skipped. Unrelated
   118	but same symptom: the Rats! temp directories in `FACTS.md` § The container.
   119	
   120	**Worktree state that is never committed.** The first repair batch forbade its
   121	workers to commit, so that the gather could compose one clean commit per rung;
   122	when the container died every worktree was dirty and four agents' work went
   123	with it. The transcript backup does not cover this: it copies JSONL, not trees,
   124	and it fires only at the main session's Stop. The fix is in the workflow design
   125	(`batched-climb-plan.md` §3, revised 2026-09-18): each worker's worktree is on
   126	its own `wip/<slug>` branch, pushed at every milestone, and the gather composes
   127	from the branch's net change instead of the dirty tree. Two rules follow for
   128	any long run: nothing that takes hours lives only on disk, and the coordinator
   129	takes a turn every 45 minutes, a series of `send_later` check-ins armed
   130	together (`FACTS.md` § The container), so that the Stop hook fires and the
   131	agents' transcripts are snapshotted while they run, and so that the session
   132	stays cached, ready to launch the next batch (Pavol, 2026-09-26 23:37 UTC,
   133	`POSITIONS-history.md`).
   134	
   135	## Setting up a batch's worktrees
   136	
   137	Since 2026-09-30 a climb batch's rung worker makes its own worktree, by the command in the batch script's shared prefix ("Your worktree"), and the coordinator makes none at the launch (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "Shared prefix"). What follows is how the first batches were set up, and how a worktree is made by hand.
   138	
   139	The workflow script cannot touch the filesystem before its first agent runs, so
   140	the coordinator creates the worktrees and pushes the empty branches first, from

140	the coordinator creates the worktrees and pushes the empty branches first, from
   141	the commit `main` is at, which is then the script's `args.base`:
   142	
   143	```sh
   144	cd /home/user/fortress && BASE=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
   145	for r in r1-atomic-static r2-literal-wrap; do
   146	  git worktree add -b wip/repair-$r /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*} main
   147	  cp -a ProjectFortress/build /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/ProjectFortress/   # javac incremental; scalac rebuilds anyway
   148	  mkdir -p /home/user/fortress-${r%%-*}/tmp
   149	  git push -u origin wip/repair-$r
   150	done
   151	```
   152	
   153	Copy the build, never symlink it: a symlinked build makes `ProjectProperties`
   154	resolve every cache path to the main tree (`batched-climb-plan.md` §4). After
   155	the batch lands, the commit stage removes the worktrees and local branches; the
   156	remote `wip/` branches are deleted in the GitHub UI.
   157	
   158	## The branch trap
   159	
   160	The infrastructure clones the branch the session was created from. If work
   161	proceeds on `main` while that branch is left behind, a re-provision lands on a
   162	stale tree — or fails outright if the branch was renamed or deleted, which is
   163	what ended the 2026-09-17 session: *"The requested branch or commit was not
   164	found in the repository."* Keep the container's own branch fast-forwarded to
   165	`main` whenever `main` moves.
   166	
   167	## Reading another session's transcript
   168	
   169	The orphan branches are in the same repository, so any session can read any
   170	other's without switching or re-cloning:
   171	
   172	```sh
   173	git fetch origin transcripts
   174	git show origin/transcripts:projects/-home-user-fortress/<session>.jsonl.parts/000.jsonl | head
   175	git grep -l 'some string' origin/transcripts -- 'projects/*'
   176	```
   177	
   178	That is enough for targeted extraction. For sustained searching, materialise it
   179	— `git worktree add /home/user/fortress-transcripts transcripts` — which costs a
   180	second on-disk copy (296 MB on 2026-09-18) and does not affect where the hook
   181	writes.
   182	
   183	## Recovering a session whose container died
   184	
   185	1. **Establish what was pushed.** `git rev-list --left-right --count <branch>...origin/main`.
   186	   Work committed before the last push is safe; nothing else in the container is.
   187	2. **Find the transcript's last record**, which bounds everything recoverable:
   188	   the tail of the last `.parts/` file, against the last snapshot commit's time.
   189	3. **Look for uncommitted edits in the tail** — mutating `Edit`/`Write`/`Bash`
   190	   tool calls after the last push. Replay them by hand if any.
   191	4. **Recover workflow scripts and briefs from the transcript.** A `Workflow`
   192	   `tool_use` record carries its whole script; that is how the repair batch's
   193	   30,751-character script was recovered on 2026-09-18.
   194	5. **Do not expect to resume a workflow run.** `resumeFromRunId` is
   195	   same-session-only and its cached agent results live in the dead session's
   196	   run state. A run designed to be extended by a later resume cannot be
   197	   finished from a new session — write the whole pipeline into one script
   198	   instead.
   199	6. **Write the handover before continuing**, from the transcript tail rather
   200	   than from memory, and record the switch in `FACTS.md`.
   201	
   202	## The 2026-09-17 incident
   203	
   204	The coordinating session (`bdff267d-…`, on `transcripts`) launched the
   205	`fortress-repair-batch` workflow at 19:26 and never reached another Stop. Its
   206	last record is 20:31:14; the snapshot six seconds later is the last one. It was
   207	still alive at about 21:07 — background tasks started then — and when it froze
   208	is not knowable from the record. Its container could not be re-provisioned
   209	because the branch it was created from was no longer found.
   210	
   211	Lost: the four workflow agents (`rung:R1`, `rung:R2`, `skeptic:R1`,
   212	`skeptic:R2`, ~798k tokens), their isolated worktrees, and the 13 hours after
   213	the last snapshot. Not lost: everything committed through `2ab1d6d8`, the
   214	workflow script, `REPAIR-BATCH.md` — written the same afternoon *"for a session
   215	that was not present"*, which is why the batch remains runnable — and the
   216	conversation through 20:31.
   217	
   218	Recovery was carried out in the blinded run's container, which already had the
   219	checkout and the toolchain: fast-forward to `main`, fix the backup, materialise
   220	the other lineage's transcripts, then re-run the batch from its recorded brief.
   221	
   222	## The 2026-09-19 interrupt
   223	
   224	A Workflow run lives inside the coordinating session's turn structure even though
   225	it is reported as a background task: when Pavol interrupted the session's turn at
   226	07:46:42 UTC, eleven seconds after a scheduled check-in had started it, both rung
   227	agents of climb batch 1 stopped at that second and the harness forgot the task
   228	(`TaskGet` returned not found). An `Agent`-tool worker launched afterwards was
   229	unaffected. Recovery was the same as after the VM restart: the `wip/` branches
   230	and the worktrees held everything pushed and everything on disk, and the batch
   231	was relaunched from the same base with the same command. Two consequences: a
   232	check-in that fires during a batch should be left to finish its turn, and,
   233	since no agent had finished, there was nothing for a resume to keep. When one
   234	has, the run is resumed with the same script text and `resumeFromRunId`, as
   235	batch 6b was on 2026-09-27 (`FACTS.md`, "A restart of the session's own
   236	process"; `resume-rule-archaeology.md`).
   237	
   238	A compaction is not an interrupt. The eight-rung climb of 2026-09-17 (run
   239	`wf_73833dfb-d25`) ran through two manual `/compact` commands, at 10:47 and 14:25
   240	UTC, both issued between turns, and completed at 14:39 with all eight rungs;
   241	the evidence is the session's archived transcript (`bdff267d`, parts file
   242	`001.jsonl`: the compact boundaries, the first post-compaction turn declining to
   243	commit "the running workflow's rung 5", and the completion notification). So
   244	while a batch runs: compact freely between turns; do not send while a turn is
   245	in flight.
   246	
   247	*Corrected 2026-09-26:* the interrupt is not a message. What stops a turn, and
   248	every background agent with it, Workflow agents and background `Agent`-tool
   249	workers alike (two workers at 2026-09-22 07:18:51, one at 2026-09-25 22:31:59), is
   250	the interrupt the transcript records as "[Request interrupted by user]"; on
   251	2026-09-26 at 12:07:47 it was very likely the iOS stop button. A message sent
   252	while a turn is in flight is queued, delivered inside the turn or as the next
   253	turn, and in eleven cases from 09-19 to 09-26 it cut no turn and killed no run. So
   254	while a batch runs: send whenever; compact between turns; do not press stop in any
   255	turn, not only a check-in.
   256	
   257	## The 2026-09-18 restart
   258	
   259	The repair batch's re-run was launched at 22:57 UTC (run `wf_9777a563-c5e`,
   260	session `fe616d40-…`). At about 23:22, 25 minutes in, the VM was restarted:
   261	the two agents' last records are 23:22:20 and 23:22:23, a test's output file
   262	was still being written at 23:22:29, and `uptime` read 0 minutes at 23:23:29
   263	on a kernel whose build string had changed (fc-v33 to fc-v37). One JVM was
   264	running across both worktrees at that moment, on 16 GB with no swap, so the
   265	load was not the cause; a platform restart is the only reading the record
   266	supports.
   267	
   268	What it cost: the two rung agents' working context, 25 minutes of two workers.
   269	What it did not cost: the disk survived, so the worktrees, their uncommitted
   270	edits, their `tmp/` logs and the agents' transcripts were all there afterwards
   271	and the transcripts were snapshotted at the next Stop; and the `wip/` branches
   272	held every milestone pushed before the restart — R1's two failing tests with
   273	their recorded failure (23:12) and its fix with the recorded pass (23:21), R2's
   274	failing test with its recorded failure (23:12). The batch was relaunched at
   275	23:28 (run `wf_aabc0cb2-d31`) from the same base, and the shared prefix gained
   276	a clause telling a worker whose branch already carries commits to read them
   277	and continue, verifying rather than redoing. The relaunched batch landed at 03:22, so the
   278	restart cost 25 minutes of two workers and nothing else.
   279	
   280	Two properties of the harness, learned here: a `Workflow` run does not survive
   281	a VM restart even when the session does — its agents are gone, the harness
   282	lists them as stopped, and `resumeFromRunId` holds nothing for an agent that
   283	never finished, so the answer was a relaunch (on 2026-09-27 a resume in the same
   284	session did recover the agents that had finished: `FACTS.md`, "A restart of the
   285	session's own process"); and a `send_later` reminder is
   286	server-side and does survive, so it is deleted or re-armed to fit the relaunch.

- A container can be lost outright: a coordinating session died mid-workflow and could not be re-provisioned, because the branch it was created from was no longer found on the remote; recovery moved into another run's container, which already had the checkout and toolchain. Cost: four workflow agents (~798k tokens), their worktrees, and the 13 hours after the last transcript snapshot; everything pushed was safe, and the batch's record kept the batch runnable. Mechanism, the three traps and the recovery procedure: `explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`.
- The transcript backup fires on the main session's Stop, not on any agent's completion, so a session inside one long turn is not being backed up. Its Stop hook returns at once (0.01 s, where every turn had waited 24-27 s plus the push) and leaves the work to a detached runner, which copies, commits, pushes whenever the branch is ahead of its upstream and packs (`gc --auto` at `gc.auto=1000`), one line per pass in `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log`, the last 200 kept; a pass takes about 10 s, the copier about 1 s of it. The copier is incremental on size and modification time (`.backup.state`), and its output is byte for byte the old copier's (1,012 files, 958 MB, `diff -r`). Workflow agents' transcripts are among its sources, and a transcript over 64 MiB is split. It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push shows only in the log's `push=` field. A container that dies within about 10 s of a turn's end loses that turn's snapshot; only an `index.lock` at least 10 s old that no process has open is cleaned, and a stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed`) until it is removed by hand. Snapshots before the change can be missing: a detached gc inherited the runner's lock and held it while it ran, and every snapshot requested meanwhile was skipped. (`transcripts-blinded@974d9be7`, its message; `coordinator/remote-container.md` § How the snapshot works; the reference copies in `coordinator/transcript-backup/`.) The platform's own Stop hook, `~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh`, comes from the launcher's `--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json` and is rewritten at every process start; it exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, whenever the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed or unverifiable commits. It is a no-op at Pavol's request, the original kept in the session scratchpad (`stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`); it returns at each restart of the process, and turning it off again is Pavol's to do in manual mode, since the auto-mode check refuses to schedule it ("The session's automatic permission check refuses a step ..." below). The push loop covers what it protected ("The push loop pushes `main` every 4 minutes ..." below).

A subagent's floor is about 45k tokens before it does anything (183k for the four). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (33,022 tokens read by agents 1–3) and not the first user message (11,010 written by each), because a cache read lands only at a breakpoint the harness placed and a shared prefix inside one message is not one. A project agent type (`.claude/agents/<name>.md`) written during the session is not found by `agent({agentType})` ("agent type ... not found") until the session's process restarts, when the registry is read. Such a type's system prompt is shared through the cache: three workflow agents of one project type whose system prompt holds about 40 KB of text (`.claude/agents/cache-probe.md`, untracked; run `wf_e2382567-828`), started one after another within a minute, the first wrote 21,070 tokens, the second and third each read 17,250 and wrote 3,820, their own message; all writes labelled five minutes. So text every agent needs, put in a project type's system prompt, is written once and read by each later agent of the type that starts within the cache's life.
- The VM can be restarted under a live session with the disk intact: worktrees, uncommitted edits and agent transcripts survive; a Workflow run and its agents do not, and the run is resumed with `resumeFromRunId` ("A restart of the session's own process kills its background runs ..." below); the `wip/` branches hold every pushed milestone (`remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart). A VM restart shows in `uptime -s` and as a `SIGTERM` in the environment manager's log at a run length that is not the cap's ("The platform stops the session's process ..." below), and the kernel build string may change (fc-v33 → fc-v37 once).

- **A message from Pavol that arrives while the coordinator is inside a turn kills a running Workflow's agents, whatever the turn is doing**: this reading is wrong. A message sent during a turn is queued, not an interrupt: it is delivered inside the turn or as the next turn, and every such message during live runs killed none, so the advice at each launch, that messages are safe, is right. The death this reading was made of was an interrupt: both agent transcripts ending at one second with "[Request interrupted by user for tool use]", the journal stopped at their `started` lines, the turn's pending Bash recorded "User rejected tool use", no message enqueued in the window, and the iOS stop button under his right thumb the likely cause (session `fe616d40`, main transcript; `subagents/workflows/wf_eb47c103-304/`).

The rule is the entry below.

- **Stopping a turn kills every background agent alive at that moment; a message sent while the coordinator is busy kills nothing** (`coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/judgement.md` § 1, from `coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/evidence.md`; session `fe616d40`, main transcript, `subagents/` and `subagents/workflows/`; session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, `001.jsonl`). Eleven messages and three `/context` commands sent while the coordinator was busy, during five live runs, killed nothing: each was queued and delivered inside the running turn or as the next turn. Five manual compactions between turns killed nothing either. That the stop button sent the interrupt is confirmed for one case in Pavol's words and very likely for another (the iOS client's stop control under his right thumb), not shown for a third; the transcripts record the effect, not the control. Not tested: an automatic compaction mid-turn, and an interrupt during the Stop hook while a run is alive. An `Agent`-tool worker killed by an interrupt cannot be resumed: a `SendMessage` to it is refused ("was stopped by the user and won't be resumed ... only launch a new agent if the user explicitly asks"), so it is relaunched only at Pavol's explicit ask, the new worker told its predecessor's leftovers (session `fe616d40`, six workers stopped by one interrupt). A restart of the session's process (`environment-manager task-run … --session-mode resume`), whether the platform's cap ("The platform stops the session's process ..." below) or a VM restart (the VM entry above), stops every Workflow run, every `Agent`-tool worker and the push loop alive at that moment. A finished agent's result is kept, an unfinished one runs from its start, and its worktree's leftovers are its starting point; a relaunch from the base restarts at the first stage instead. - The disk allowance fills with parser-generation temp directories: every run that imports a grammar generates a Rats! parser into a fresh `/tmp/fortress<random>rats` directory (`RatsUtil.getTempDir`, `syntax_abstractions/rats/RatsUtil.java:138-146`, via `IOUtil.createAndMarkTempDirectory`), 5.8 MB each, never deleted; 723 of them (4.2 GB) filled the allowance on 2026-09-15 and broke a worker's tool output mid-run ("no space left on device"). Deficit until fixed at the source (an edit to the original tree, or a `deleteOnExit`); mitigation in our tree: `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them when sourced, and `df` must be checked before any long run.
----
     1	# The machine and its prices
     2	
     3	Facts about this container and the tools on it, with numbers. They were checked against `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` (its test-harness and container sections), the files it cites, `explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`, the header lines of the two measurement scripts and the last full run's summary. Times are wall-clock seconds on this machine; a run beside other work is slower.
     4	
     5	## The machine
     6	
     7	- **CPUs: 4** (Intel Xeon at 2.8 GHz, `nproc` = 4); about 15 GB of memory (`free -g`, measured now). OpenJDK 25. The suites pin one interpreter thread per JVM (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, set in `build.xml`), so the four cores are used by running several JVMs at once (`ant testFast` runs four tracks that occupy the four cores; `ant testSystem` is split into four shards).
     8	- **Heaps.** `bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set; the `ant testSystem` harness 768 MB; `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, which every measurement script expects to be sourced, sets 4 GB.
     9	- **Disk.** Every run that imports a grammar writes a 5.8 MB parser directory to `/tmp` (`/tmp/fortress<random>rats`) and never deletes it; 723 of them (4.2 GB) once filled the disk allowance and broke a tool's output with "no space left on device". Sourcing `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them; check `df` before a long run.
    10	- **Build commands.** `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, `export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH`, `export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>`, `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, then `ant compileAll` from the repository root. `ant compileAll` deletes the whole `default_repository/caches` including the tracked file `default_repository/caches/global.map`: restore it with `git checkout -- default_repository/caches/global.map` after every `ant compileAll`, and never commit its deletion. A compiled run (`fortress compile`, `fortress run`) needs the library compiled in order after a rebuild (AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary, CompilerAlgebra, CompilerSystem); stale caches give a misleading `NoSuchMethodError`. Walk does not need that order; its first run warms its own caches.
    11	
    12	## The times
    13	
    14	- `ant compileAll`: 57 s in the last full run; 82 s on a fresh checkout; 25 to 40 s on an already built tree after a small edit.
    15	- The library compile (the five components in order, after `ant compileAll`): 108 to 112 s (AnyType 17, CompilerBuiltin 63, CompilerLibrary 27, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 2); one component alone 2 to 63 s. A base built from nothing, `ant compileAll` plus the library compile plus one walk run, is about 200 s.
    16	- `ant testFast`: 635 s (10 min 35 s) in the last full run, 1,782 tests, 0 failures; the longest single suite in it takes about 440 s, so more parallelism does not shorten it much.
    17	- `ant testSystem`: 243 s (4 min 3 s) in the last full run, 504 tests in four shards, 0 failures.
    18	- The checker-count measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]`; it counts the errors the compiled checker reports on the library before each api's early return, 1 now): about 20 s alone on an idle machine when first measured (the library has grown since); 139 s when it ran beside other jobs.
    19	- The distance measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]`; it runs every phase of the compiled checker over all twelve apis and twelve components in one JVM on one busy core and counts every distinct error, 340 now): 1,212 s (20 min) in the last full run, 732 s of it on `FortressLibrary` alone; 789 s on an idle machine earlier; 14 to 24 minutes under load.
    20	- One walk run of a small program: about 8 s on cold caches. A compile of a small program: about 5 s, its run about 1 s.
    21	
    22	## Copying a build, and running the old code
    23	
    24	- **A built tree can be copied into a new worktree in about 3 s**: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]`. The base worktree must have been built once (`ant compileAll`, the restore of `global.map`, the library compile). The copy (206 MB: build 40 MB, caches 36 MB) runs walk and the compiled path without building anything, and its paths are translated for the new location.
    25	- **The base's code runs beside the new code** with a private cache folder: `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...` (for example `old-fortress.sh <base-build> <dir>/old-caches compile P.fss`, then `... run P`, or `... P.fss` for walk). The private folder is a copy of the base's caches, 36 MB made in 0.04 s; the run writes nothing that stays in the base build. Keep the private folder and the programs outside the base build.
    26	
    27	## The agents and their prices
    28	
    29	- **How many agents run at once: 2.** The multi-agent harness (the script-driven tool that starts agents in parallel or in sequence) runs two agents at a time on this box; more wait for a free slot.
    30	- **An agent's floor is about 45,000 tokens before it does anything** (system prompt, tools, first message). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (about 33,000 tokens read) and not the first user message (about 11,000 tokens written by each agent). Agents started with an identical whole prompt share the cache (the second reads what the first wrote and writes nothing); a prompt that differs only in its last line shares only the system prompt and tools (about 35,000 tokens read) and writes the rest again.
    31	- **The prompt cache lives 1 hour for the main session and 5 minutes for a subagent.** A call within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait taken in steps shorter than the life costs a cache read per step. A wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again with no cache read: a subagent holding a 250,000-token context that waits 8 minutes on a build writes 250,000 tokens at its next call.
    32	- **The Bash tool's time limit is 10 minutes** (600 s) for a foreground call (default 2 minutes); the call is killed at the limit. A longer command runs in the background and is polled.
    33	- **The project counts cost as tokens written**: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
    34	- **Three model tiers are available: Opus, Sonnet and Fable.** Fable is the strongest and draws on a separate, scarcer weekly pool; Sonnet is the cheapest. An agent that names no model inherits the session's.
    35	- **An agent call can come back empty.** The harness returns null for an agent it has marked failed, even when the agent delivered its structured result first (the platform's safety filter has ended agents this way); a design must expect it.
    36	- **The platform stops the session's process after about 13 hours** (12 h 58 min of continuous running; the stops fall at 46,636 to 46,660 s) and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. The restart kills every running harness run and every running agent; the conversation, the worktrees, the transcripts and each run's journal survive. **A run of the harness is resumed from its journal**: agents that had finished keep their results, an unfinished agent runs again from its start. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's agent calls in call order, so it needs the script and its arguments exactly as at launch and the agents called in the same order. A VM restart and an interrupt of the session's current turn also kill running agents; a resume from the journal recovers the harness's agents that had finished.
